how-to-teach-body-safety-to-children:
Body safety is taught in ordinary language, calmly, over years. It is not one conversation, it does not require frightening a child, and the aim is not vigilance. The aim is a child who knows their body is theirs and who tells you things.

Start with the words

Use anatomical names for body parts from the beginning, in the same tone as elbow and knee. This is the single most recommended step by safeguarding organisations, for a practical reason: a child who has family nicknames for private parts cannot report clearly, and an adult who hears a nickname may not understand what is being described.

It also communicates something quieter. Parts of the body that cannot be named are parts a child learns not to talk about.

Four ideas, repeated in ordinary moments

Your body belongs to you. Practised in small ways long before it matters: not forcing hugs or kisses for relatives, letting a child stop a tickling game the moment they say stop, and stopping immediately when they do. A child who has been overruled on this a hundred times has learned that their no does not count.

Some parts are private. The parts covered by underwear. Adults do not need to look at or touch them except for health or hygiene, and then they say why.

Secrets about bodies are not allowed. This is the most useful single rule available, because grooming almost always involves a secret. Distinguish surprises, which are fun and get told, from secrets you are supposed to keep for ever, which are not allowed in this family.

You can always tell me, and you will never be in trouble for telling. Say the second half out loud. Children commonly stay quiet because they believe they will be blamed, or because they were told something bad would happen.

Who to tell

Help them name three or four trusted adults, including at least one outside the household. This matters because most harm comes from somebody known to the family, and a child whose only route is through the household may have no route at all.

Tone

Matter of fact. In the car, at bath time, folded into ordinary life rather than delivered as a serious talk. A frightened child does not become safer; they become less likely to raise something, because they can see it upsets you.

And avoid teaching that danger comes from strangers, which is both inaccurate and misdirects the attention.

What makes a child likelier to tell

Everything ordinary. A household where small worries get taken seriously, where the response to bad news is help rather than a lecture, and where a child has been believed before. That is built years earlier on subjects that have nothing to do with safety.

If you are worried about a specific child, contact your local child protection service or a specialist helpline rather than acting alone. This page is general guidance and is not a safeguarding assessment.
good-touch-and-bad-touch-for-kids:
The good touch, bad touch framing is well intentioned and safeguarding specialists have largely moved away from it. It is worth understanding why, because the gaps are not obvious and they are the gaps that matter.

Where it fails

Harmful touch does not always feel bad. This is the central problem. Grooming is frequently gentle and pleasant, and a child taught that bad touch feels bad concludes that what is happening cannot be the thing they were warned about. Worse, they may feel they have done something wrong because it did not feel unpleasant.

Necessary touch can feel bad. Medicine, an injection, having a splinter removed, being cleaned when unwell. A child working from the feeling alone gets these wrong in the other direction.

It puts the judgement on the child. A four-year-old is asked to classify adult behaviour by how it feels, which is a heavy thing to hand them and not something they can reliably do.

What is used instead

Rules about bodies and secrets, which do not depend on a child interpreting a feeling.

Body ownership. Your body is yours. You decide about hugs and kisses. Nobody continues when you say stop.

Private parts. The parts under underwear. Adults do not look at or touch them except for health or hygiene, and they say why when they do.

The secrets rule. Surprises get told in the end and are fun. Secrets you must keep for ever are not allowed here. If any adult asks you to keep one, tell me and you will not be in trouble.

The safe adults list. Three or four people, including one outside the house.

The secrets rule is the most useful of the four, because it targets the mechanism rather than asking a child to assess a feeling.

The uh-oh feeling still has a place

Teaching a child to notice when something feels off, and to act on it without needing to justify it, remains worth doing. What changes is that it sits alongside the rules rather than instead of them, and it is framed as permission rather than as a detection method: if something feels wrong you may leave, say no, or come and tell me, and you do not have to explain why.

The part most likely to matter

Whether your child brings you difficult news at all. That is decided by every earlier occasion when they brought you something small and were met with help rather than anger, panic or a lecture.

If you are worried about a specific child, contact your local child protection service or a specialist helpline. This page is general guidance and is not a safeguarding assessment.
safety-rules-every-child-should-know:
A short list, with the age each rule can genuinely be understood rather than merely repeated. A rule a child can recite and cannot apply is not protection.

Getting lost

From about three: stay exactly where you are, or find a person who works here. The instruction to stay still is more useful than any description of who to approach, because a moving child and a searching adult can miss each other for a long time.

From about five: know their own full name, a parent's full name and a phone number. Practise it as a song or a rhythm; it survives panic better that way.

Who to approach: somebody in a uniform, somebody behind a till, or a woman with children. Not the first adult who offers. This is worth teaching as a preference order rather than a rule about strangers.

Roads

From three: hold a hand or the buggy near a road, every time, no negotiation.

From five: stop at the kerb, look and listen, cross with an adult. They can lead the routine while you stay with them.

From eight or nine: some children can cross quiet roads alone. Judging the speed of an approaching car is a skill that is genuinely not mature until around ten, which is the reason the age is later than it feels.

Water

Any age: never near water without an adult who is watching, not one who is nearby. Drowning is fast and almost silent, which is not intuitive.

From about four: swimming lessons, and the rule that they ask before going in.

People

From three: the body and secrets rules. Your body is yours, private parts are private, no adult asks a child to keep a secret from their parents, and you will never be in trouble for telling.

From five: the safe adults list, including one outside the household.

Note what is absent: stranger danger. Most harm comes from somebody known, and the stranger framing points a child's attention in the wrong direction while making the world frightening.

Home

From five: how to call emergency services, what to say, and the address. Practise it.

From six or seven: what to do if there is a fire. Get out, stay out, do not fetch anything.

Medicines and cleaning products: never taken or touched without an adult, whatever they look like.

How to teach any of it

Rehearse rather than lecture. Walk to the corner and practise the crossing routine. Ask what they would do if they turned round in the shop and you were gone. Do it calmly and repeatedly, in ordinary moments.

A rule that has been practised is available under stress. A rule that has only been explained usually is not.
internet-safety-rules-for-kids:
Rules a child can actually follow, at the age each becomes meaningful. The important thing about this list is the last section, which explains why rules alone stop working at exactly the point they matter most.

Under about seven

The rules here are for the adult, not the child. Devices in shared rooms, content chosen rather than searched, autoplay off, no open comment sections. A child this age cannot evaluate what they meet, so the design of the environment is the whole intervention.

The one rule worth teaching directly: come and get me if anything is confusing or upsetting, and you will not be in trouble.

Seven to eleven

  • Personal details stay private: full name, school, address, phone number, and photographs that show any of them.
  • People online are not always who they say. Explained plainly and without drama.
  • Never arrange to meet somebody from online. Tell me instead if they suggest it.
  • Ask before downloading or installing anything.
  • If something is upsetting, leave it and tell me. Not close it and hide it.
  • Be someone you would be happy for me to see being. Better than a rule about kindness, because it is checkable.

Eleven and up

  • Anything sent can be kept and forwarded. Including things that promise to disappear.
  • Never send images of yourself, and tell me if you are asked. Say explicitly that you will help rather than punish. Fear of the reaction is the main reason this goes unreported.
  • Blocking and reporting are normal. Show them where the buttons are rather than describing them.
  • Check what a thing is before believing it. Who made this, and what do they get from me seeing it.
  • Passwords are not shared, including with friends.

Why rules stop being enough

Because by thirteen or fourteen, a child has more access than you can restrict, more skill at routing around restrictions than most parents expect, and a social life that lives on those platforms. Rules that depend on control fail quietly at that point, and the failure is invisible.

What continues to work is the relationship. Specifically, whether a child believes they can bring you a problem without losing their phone, being shouted at, or being told they should have known better.

That belief is built years earlier, on smaller things. The single most protective sentence available to you is that you will help first and be angry later if at all, said before anything has happened and then honoured the first time it is tested.

If you are worried about a specific situation, contact your local child protection service or a specialist online safety helpline.
